title: I Went to a Music Festival in the Malaysian Rainforest
excerpt: It is more than a gathering for music fans. A whole city is pinning its hopes for tourism on it.
body:
It is more than a gathering for music fans. A whole city is pinning its hopes for tourism on it.

On my second day in Malaysia, the country's biggest English-language newspaper, *The Star*, reported on its front page that wreckage from Malaysia Airlines had been confirmed found. On day 515 of a search that drew on rescue teams from 26 countries, debris from the missing MH370 had finally washed up on the shore of Réunion, a French island.

People call what happened to Malaysia Airlines in 2014 "terrible luck." After two air disasters in quick succession, the airline, which had been losing money for years, faced an even graver threat to its survival. Only at the end of the year, when the government's investment fund Khazanah Nasional bought it for US$1.66 billion, did news of a restructuring arrive.

The crashes also cast a shadow over tourism, because the airline belongs to the Malaysian government. In 2013, about 1.558 million Chinese tourists entered Malaysia; by July 2014 that number had fallen by 11.8%.

This may be why Malaysia decided to name 2015

the "Year of Festivals."

From the Langkawi International Regatta to a festival of Muslim culture to a mask festival, this country of 329,000 square kilometers now stages an average of eight festivals of different kinds every month. On the AirAsia X flight I took from Shanghai to Kuala Lumpur, the seat backs, unsurprisingly, were covered in Year of Festivals ads.

It is easy to guess what the government hopes to gain by packing festivals together to revive tourism. But apart from these hastily assembled "festivals," in Kuching, the capital of Sarawak state and far from the national capital, the Rainforest World Music Festival ran from August 7 to 9. Now in its 18th consecutive year, it was the reason for my trip.

### 1.

Like any music festival, the Rainforest World Music Festival puts its two stages on a wide, open field. The difference is that behind the stages rises a dense tropical rainforest, Mount Santubong.

The forest lies within the Sarawak Cultural Village, a 40-minute drive from downtown Kuching, with the South China Sea close by. On ordinary days the village charges admission, which pays for its upkeep. Rainforest covers 70% of Sarawak, but apart from a few remote national parks, the forest at the Cultural Village is the closest to the city and the easiest for visitors to enjoy.

Since 2010, the British music magazine Songlines has repeatedly named the festival one of the world's 25 best, and it is the largest music festival in Malaysia. This year 24 bands performed, from Mongolia, Poland, Tunisia and Sarawak's indigenous communities, among other places. Among the acts that got the crowd going were some whose instruments, singing styles and religious tribal music had a strong folk character.

![Performers on stage at the Rainforest World Music Festival](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160450fi78yaTSv1eVuFnm.jpg-w600)

![A band performing at the festival](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160450tH2Luep0ars9mwj1.jpg-w600)

![Musicians at the festival](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016060716045140rRTywp2JlnVguW.jpg-w600)![The festival crowd](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160451AOvTnG0zLjxYqR7y.jpg-w600)

![A performance at the Rainforest World Music Festival](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160452KPyvtSbGHZWRoCzn.jpg-w600)

Besides the concerts, which run every night from 7:30 until past midnight, the bands also hold workshops, where they explain their instruments and the stories behind their styles, or simply improvise a tune.

According to official figures, 20,000 people attended this year, roughly as expected.

Howard Martyn, a Canadian who teaches English at City University of Hong Kong, was at the festival for the third time. A friend in Kuching had recommended it to him back in 2001. "Before I came here I hadn't actually listened to much world music, but once I came, I found I liked it," Martyn told me. He returned in 2006, and he still passes word of the festival on to friends.

"A world music festival is a great thing. It lets folk and tribal music that only a few people listen to survive on a commercial footing. And at a big event like this we get to see these small bands play, and it shows us another side of music," Martyn said.

![Howard Martyn](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160452xkodMBNJ1ieRWFVy.jpg-w600)Howard Martyn

Apart from a lax security check at the gate and the lack of separate smoking and non-smoking areas, Martyn's other small complaint was getting there. On the festival's opening day he boarded an AirAsia flight in Hong Kong at 11 a.m., landed in Kuala Lumpur, changed planes and reached Kuching at 7:20 p.m. He still had to catch a shuttle bus to the Cultural Village, which meant missing some of the performances.

"Changing planes isn't really a hassle, but a direct flight would be better," Martyn said.

For any place trying to build tourism, easy transport is the first thing to get right. For now, it seems to be a headache for both the Sarawak state government and the festival.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), Kuching is Malaysia's second-busiest passenger airport after Kuala Lumpur. Every day more than 20 AirAsia flights, 10 Malaysia Airlines flights and three Malindo Air flights fly from Kuala Lumpur to Kuching.

State-owned Malaysia Airlines is one of the festival's sponsors, but the airline with the most flights is in fact AirAsia, a private low-cost carrier founded in 2001 (the festival's fourth year). To some extent AirAsia has also brought Kuching closer to the outside world. After it opened a Guangzhou-Kuala Lumpur route in 2008, it began carrying Chinese tourists, directly and indirectly, to this little-known Malaysian town.

Even so, the only international direct flights into Kuching still come from neighbors such as Singapore, Brunei and Indonesia, and that is far from enough.

At a press briefing during the festival, Sarawak's minister of tourism and housing, Datuk Amar Abang Johari, was asked about direct flights. He said the federal government had agreed that the Sarawak and Sabah state governments would jointly take over MASwings, a wholly owned subsidiary of Malaysia Airlines.

### 2.

"We never thought about doing a rock or pop festival. With the rainforest behind us, we wanted to do something special. Otherwise, why would anyone fly all the way out here?" said Liu Huixin, East Asia regional manager in the marketing department of the Sarawak Tourism Board. She moved back to Kuching from Australia and has helped organize the festival for 10 years.

Rather than a gathering for music fans, the festival, run by the Sarawak state government, is on one hand a big party with music and on the other Kuching's star tourist attraction, with an appeal that reaches well beyond music lovers.

The pitch works. At least one of my fellow travelers sighed, "Listening to tribal music in the rainforest really does suit Malaysia, with its complicated society and its unspoiled nature."

![The festival grounds at the edge of the rainforest](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160453HYjAtvl4SQuJpG3i.jpg-w600)

Unlike the familiar Kuala Lumpur, Sarawak lies across the South China Sea on another island, Borneo. This region, far more thinly populated than the Malay Peninsula, is known as West Malaysia; together with Sabah, also part of Malaysia, and Brunei, it makes up what is called the "three states of northern Borneo." Besides the capital Kuching, there is Miri, Malaysia's first oil-producing town, where oil is still the main industry. Elsewhere, as across much of Southeast and South Asia, the state exports large quantities of spices, pepper among them.

The largest ethnic group in Sarawak is the Iban, a branch of the Dayak, Borneo's indigenous people. Ethnic Chinese come second and Malays third. Beyond these, Sarawak alone has 27 ethnic groups, large and small. Some still live in the rainforest, in a way little known to outsiders, rather like the life described in *The Innocent Anthropologist*. Some live in traditional longhouses built by the water, now tourist attractions, and some moved to the cities long ago. At the Sarawak State Museum we saw both traditional Iban funerary objects and animal specimens hunted and mounted by early British colonists. The museum reads like a vivid early work of natural history, and behind it lies, without question, a great diversity of cultures.

![Map showing Kuching as a blue dot](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160453RrsqUDtSgEd1JLCy.jpg-w600)Kuching is the blue dot

![Inside a longhouse](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160453gHyx8hFw2OdXiDSQ.jpg-w600)Inside a longhouse

Sarawak's 32 national parks, meanwhile, are home to proboscis monkeys, hornbills, wild boar and more than 70 endangered mammal species. There is not a single zoo here, yet the wild itself gives many people the animals they imagined.

So almost every official Sarawak tourism publication puts the rainforest's plants and animals, indigenous people in striking dress, and the word "Adventure" front and center. To modern people who complain of being trapped in concrete cities, this kind of experience looks attractive.

### 3.

"Tourism in Kuching used to be very quiet, with no big events. But the rainforest festival made a lot of people realize there's a place called Sarawak and a city called Kuching," Zhuo Jiaqi told me. Our guide on this trip, she has worked in local tourism for 14 years. She is the daughter of Fujianese immigrants and speaks Malay, Cantonese and Mandarin.

In Malay, Kuching means "cat," so the city has plenty of cat statues and even a cat museum. But because many of the early immigrants were Chinese, the city's Chinese name sounds like the Chinese for "old well."

Walking down Kuching's Attap Street feels like stepping into a Wong Kar-wai film. A temple festival we stumbled on one evening at the Siew San Teng Tua Pek Kong Temple made us feel we were somewhere in Guangdong.

![An old street in Kuching](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606071604540ZblQs2uTMJyfNp4.jpg-w600)Kuching's old street

Kuching has only 650,000 people, fewer than a single district of Shanghai, yet it is split into two cities, north and south, each with its own mayor. The south is home to ethnic Chinese, mostly Hakka and Hokkien, the north to Malays. Back in the 1970s, Malays lived in the south too, but they found their way of life very different from that of the Chinese, and many moved north. So although society here is complicated, it is fundamentally different from places that saw events like the anti-Chinese violence in Indonesia in 1998.

In a sense, Kuching, which became a city only in 1988, is still at a fairly early stage. Five or six years ago, foot-massage parlors spread from mainland China to Kuching for the first time. For a while their signs were everywhere, and men and women alike went in out of curiosity. The boom has passed and the craze has cooled, but the fact that one industry could change the look of the city shows, indirectly, that the city has not yet matured.

Zhuo Jiaqi is one of Kuching's 130 registered tour guides, and at almost every sight we visited she ran into someone she knew from the trade. She does not work for any travel agency; when an agency gets a booking, it simply phones her to lead the group.

Kuching's guide licensing exam is less developed than mainland China's. There is no set material to memorize, and candidates mostly have to gather and prepare their own. Zhuo Jiaqi had meant to become an office clerk, but she passed the exam and drifted into guiding by chance. Now she does her old job while also working in the hottest trade of the moment, real estate. "You can't make a living from this line of work alone," she said.

All this seems to show three things. First, Kuching's tourism circle is small. Second, its sights are so similar that it has not come close to offering tailor-made tours, so the industry is still basic. Third, if it does take off, local tourism may have a lot of room to grow.

After more than a decade of running the festival, Kuching has finally begun to reap what it sowed. More and more Western visitors like Howard Martyn have been drawn to Kuching by the festival. High-rises, star-rated hotels, Western restaurants such as Junk and Barber, and boutique hotels that trade on individuality have multiplied in their wake.

![A street scene in Kuching](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160455r6NdhF7aWYESDB4i.jpg-w600)

"Western tourists feel their own countries are too built-up, not natural like ours. Things are cheap in Kuching and the exchange rate is good, so they're happy to come," Zhuo Jiaqi told me.

Tourism, as a starting point, is changing the whole life of the city.

### 4.

Kuching used to see the Chinese-speaking world mostly through Taiwan. At the Kuching food festival, held at the same time as the music festival, the words "Taiwanese food" appeared again and again. In Zhuo Jiaqi's father's generation, Taiwan sent Kuching many entertainers, including Chin Han and Brigitte Lin, and Teresa Teng sang in Kuching before she became famous. Today the ties are kept alive by Taiwanese idol dramas and by local singers such as Nicholas Teo and Rynn Lim, who went to Taiwan to build their careers.

But it is a fact, not a plug or a joke, that *The Voice of China* has connected more and more Kuching people with mainland China. "A lot of people here follow it religiously. It airs here as long as the stations have signed Chinese-language broadcast agreements," Zhuo Jiaqi told me.

Meanwhile, the Malaysian government has in recent years pushed its "Malaysia My Second Home" (MM2H) visa program, which gives foreigners who meet certain conditions a multiple-entry social visit pass. Drawn by the incentives, more and more Chinese companies have begun buying property in Kuching, which also feeds the real estate business Zhuo Jiaqi now runs on the side.

It is close to common knowledge that mainland Chinese consumers have become indispensable to the growth of many industries.

When it comes to tourism aimed purely at Chinese visitors, Sarawak's direct rival is not Kuala Lumpur but Sabah, also on the West Malaysia peninsula.

Sabah's towns, including Kota Kinabalu, Semporna and Kapalai, and its sun, beaches and diving are already familiar to many travelers. On Qyer.com, the Sabah travel guide has been downloaded 300,000 times, while neither Sarawak nor Kuching even makes the top 10 on the Malaysia list. Partly to set itself apart, Sarawak avoided the character used for "Sa" in Sabah's Chinese name and chose a different one for its own. But in July 2014, armed militants attacked Mabul Island off Semporna in Sabah, leaving tourists with a lingering worry about safety there.

"The focus of our promotion is eco-tourism," Liu Huixin said.

In China, the Sarawak Tourism Board has accounts on both Weibo and WeChat. Wang Chuan, who runs its on-the-ground promotion in China, was the very first follower of the board's Weibo account when it was set up in 2013.

"When I first went to Sarawak in 2013, the only tourist I saw was one person from Taiwan. But even then I thought that if it were promoted well, Sarawak could become as popular as Sabah," Wang Chuan said.

![Rainforest scenery in Sarawak](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607160455QcarMh1o7dJkUn6D.jpg-w600)

Since last year, he has worked with travel sites such as Lailaihui and Youduoduo to run several rounds of Sarawak promotions in Beijing, Guangzhou and Tianjin. "The rainforest festival is the main thing we pitch, and we also introduce Sarawak's food, lodging and transport. We want people to consider Sarawak when they're planning an independent trip abroad," Wang Chuan said.

Independent travel abroad is growing steadily. According to Qyer.com's "2014 Outbound Independent Travel Industry Report," more than 70% of China's 109 million outbound travelers chose to travel independently. The Sarawak Tourism Board sees this as exactly the trend to ride.

On Wang Chuan's timetable, the board will team up with more online travel agencies (OTAs) by the end of the year, and he is also urging the festival to invite performers from China. All of it rests on one hope: that more people holding Chinese passports will come to Sarawak.

"Chinese visitors who once loved shopping are taking to eco-tourism," is how *Sin Chew Daily*, Malaysia's largest-circulation Chinese-language newspaper, summed up where Sarawak tourism is heading. The day after I got home, Liu Huixin posted a photo on WeChat Moments filled with Western tourists. Her caption read: "Most of Sarawak's visitors are people like them. We hope to see Chinese tourists here soon too."
